name: Scaling Laws and Model Size
intent: Understand how model quality changes with parameters, data and compute, and how a fixed training budget is best split between a bigger model and more text.
scenario: A team has budget for one large training run. They must decide between a very large model trained on a modest amount of text and a smaller model trained on much more, and they know that whichever they pick will also have to be served to users for years.
problem: Training a large language model costs a fixed amount of compute, and the result cannot be repeated casually. Compute can go into a bigger model or into more training tokens, and putting it all into one of them wastes it. Guessing wrongly gives a model that is bigger than it needs to be, or one that was stopped long before it had learned what its size allows.

howItWorks.title: Loss falls as a power law
howItWorks.text: Kaplan and colleagues measured the cross-entropy loss of language models of many sizes. They found that it falls off as a power law with model size, with dataset size and with the compute used, in some trends over more than seven orders of magnitude. Improvements are smooth, and each one costs more than the last.

howItWorks.title: Compute is about 6 x parameters x tokens
howItWorks.text: A common approximation for the cost of training is C = 6 x N x D floating-point operations, where N is the number of parameters and D the number of training tokens. For a fixed budget C, a larger N means a smaller D. The choice of N is the choice of how many tokens the model will see.

howItWorks.title: Early advice: big models, modest data
howItWorks.text: The 2020 study found that larger models are more sample-efficient, so a compute-efficient run trains a very large model on a relatively modest amount of data and stops well before convergence. Several large models were trained that way.

howItWorks.title: Chinchilla: scale both together
howItWorks.text: Hoffmann and colleagues trained over 400 models and concluded that model size and training tokens should grow in equal proportion. They tested this with Chinchilla, 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens with the same compute as Gopher, a model four times larger trained on fewer tokens. Chinchilla did better on a wide range of tasks.

howItWorks.title: About 20 tokens per parameter
howItWorks.text: Chinchilla's own numbers are 1.4 trillion tokens for 70 billion parameters, which is 20 tokens for every parameter, and about 20 is the figure usually quoted as the rule of thumb. It is a result of curve fitting, not a law of nature, and different ways of fitting give somewhat different answers. With C = 6 x N x D and D = 20 x N, the best N for a budget is the square root of C / 120.

howItWorks.title: Serving changes the answer
howItWorks.text: Training happens once, but every generated token costs roughly in proportion to the number of parameters, again and again. A team that expects heavy use may train a smaller model on far more tokens than the training-optimal ratio, accepting a higher training bill for a cheaper model to run.

pros: Smooth, predictable trends let a team estimate the result of a run before paying for it
A rule for splitting compute avoids the worst mistakes: an oversized, undertrained model
Small test runs can be extrapolated to guide a large one
The same reasoning applies to deciding how much data to collect
cons: The laws describe loss on text prediction, not usefulness on a particular task
Fitted constants and exponents depend on the data, the architecture and the fitting method
They say little about data quality, repeated data or running out of fresh text
They optimise the cost of training and ignore the cost of serving unless you add it
whenToUse: You are judging whether a model claim, such as a size and a token count, is reasonable
You are planning how to split a training budget between size and data
You are explaining why a smaller, longer-trained model can beat a larger one
whenNotToUse: Do not treat 20 tokens per parameter as a law: it is a rule of thumb from fits
Do not use training-optimal ratios when serving cost dominates the total
Do not read the loss curve as a promise about accuracy on your own task
pitfalls: Assuming a model ten times bigger is ten times better on a task
Comparing parameter counts without comparing training tokens
Extrapolating a fitted curve far beyond the sizes it was measured on
Forgetting that high-quality text is limited and that repeating it has diminishing returns

roles.label: Compute budget
roles.description: The total number of floating-point operations the team can spend on training.

roles.label: Model size
roles.description: The number of parameters, N. It also sets the cost of serving each token.

roles.label: Training tokens
roles.description: How much text the model sees, D. For a fixed budget, more data means a smaller model.

roles.label: Loss
roles.description: How well the model predicts text. It falls smoothly, with diminishing returns, as the budget grows.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

quiz.question: A team has a fixed compute budget and plans to train the biggest model it can afford on a small dataset. According to the compute-optimal results, what is the most likely problem?
options: The model will be too small, because large datasets always require larger models
The model will be undertrained: for that budget, a smaller model trained on more tokens would reach a lower loss
The budget will be wasted, because loss does not improve as models get bigger
The model will memorise the dataset, which makes training faster for the same budget
quiz.explanation: The Chinchilla study found that earlier large models were too big for the amount of data they saw. For a fixed budget, model size and tokens should grow together, so a smaller model with more data does better. Loss does improve with size, and the problem is the split, not the size alone.

quiz.question: A company expects its model to answer billions of requests. Why might it train a smaller model on far more tokens than the compute-optimal ratio suggests?
options: Because the laws say that a smaller model always has a lower loss than a bigger one
Because extra tokens make a model cheaper to train, whatever its size or budget
Because compute-optimal ratios cannot be calculated for models of a few billion parameters
Because serving cost grows with the number of parameters, so a smaller model that was trained for longer can be cheaper overall
quiz.explanation: The compute-optimal ratio minimises the cost of training for a given loss. If a model will be run enormous numbers of times, the cost of each generated token matters more, and spending extra training compute on a smaller model can lower the total cost.

quiz.question: A team reads that loss falls as a power law with compute and concludes that a model ten times bigger will be ten times better on their task. What is wrong with this?
options: The laws describe smooth, diminishing gains in loss on text, not a proportional gain on a particular task
Power laws only apply to models smaller than a billion parameters, so they say nothing about large ones
The laws say that a bigger model is always worse, so the conclusion is the wrong way round
The laws only describe training speed, so they cannot be used to compare model sizes at all
quiz.explanation: The measured trend is in cross-entropy loss, and it flattens as compute grows: each step of improvement costs more than the last. How much a task improves depends on the task and is not proportional to size. The laws were measured over many orders of magnitude of size, and they do describe size comparisons.
